reference.title: Lying Single Leg Raise (male)
reference.listing: Page could not be read (gymvisual.com is blocked by the network proxy); movement taken from the exercise name and standard coaching practice

breathing.pattern: Exhale as the leg rises, inhale as it lowers.
breathing.cadence: About 1.4 s up, short pause, about 2 s down

prescription.tempo: About 1.5 s up, brief pause, 2 s down; heel hovers between reps
prescription.progression: Slower lowering, then both legs together (lying leg raise)

cues.text: Lie flat, arms by your sides palms down, both legs straight; lift one heel just off the mat.
Breathe out and raise the straight leg to about vertical; the other leg stays long on the mat.
Brief pause with the foot over the hip; pelvis level and low back down.
Breathe in and lower slowly until the heel hovers.
Finish the set, then switch legs.

mistakes.mistake: The resting leg lifts or bends as the working leg rises
mistakes.fix: Press the resting leg into the mat and keep it long.

mistakes.mistake: Pelvis tilting or the low back arching
mistakes.fix: Brace and lower only as far as the back stays flat.
Start from a still hover and lift smoothly.

mistakes.mistake: Bending the working knee a lot to get higher
mistakes.fix: Keep the knee long; stop where the hamstrings allow.

kinematics.norm: From a hover to about vertical, as far as the hamstrings allow (clinical opinion)
Rises to about 90 degrees at the top (clinical opinion)
Pelvis and the resting leg stay still (clinical opinion)
About 1.5 s up and 2-3 s down (clinical opinion)

sources.title: GymVisual #23830, Lying Single Leg Raise (male), video (movement reference; page not readable here)

McGill 1998, low back exercises: evidence for improving exercise regimens (Phys Ther 78(7):754-765; PMID 9672547)
Clark, Holt and Sinyard 2003, electromyographic comparison of the upper and lower rectus abdominis during abdominal exercises (J Strength Cond Res 17(3):475-483; PMID 12930172)
Axler and McGill 1997, low-back loads over a variety of abdominal exercises: searching for the safest abdominal challenge (Med Sci Sports Exerc 29(6):804-811)

cautions: Stop if you feel sharp, radiating or nerve-type pain.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
A one-leg raise loads the low back much less than raising both legs; if the back still arches, bend the resting knee with the foot flat.
Low-back pain or disc problems: prefer bent-knee raises, dead bugs or curl-ups.
Pregnancy and postpartum (diastasis recti): get individual guidance before dynamic trunk-flexion or straight-leg work.
modify: Bend the knees to shorten the lever.
Hands under the hips if the low back lifts.
Shorter range: stop lowering higher up.
regressions: Bend the resting knee, foot flat on the mat.

muscleNotes.hip_flexors_r: Iliopsoas and rectus femoris lift and lower the leg. A unilateral leg lift needs far less abdominal work than a bilateral one (Andersson 1997).
muscleNotes.core: Rectus abdominis and the deep abdominals hold the pelvis steady; unilateral lifts needed little abdominal activation in Andersson 1997.
muscleNotes.quads_r: Keeps the knee straight; rectus femoris also flexes the hip.
muscleNotes.obliques_r: Stops the pelvis tilting and rotating as one leg rises (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.obliques_l: Stops the pelvis tilting and rotating as one leg rises (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_l: Quiet; the resting leg stays on the mat.
muscleNotes.glute_max_l: Presses the resting leg lightly into the mat to anchor the pelvis (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.hamstrings_r: Lengthen as the straight leg approaches vertical; tight hamstrings limit the top of the range.
